questions.text: I notice when a group instinctively leaves a chair empty next to someone they find socially difficult.
A smell connected to a past experience can instantly transport me into the full emotional state of that time.
I create project timelines with specific milestones and check-in points.
When someone shares a painful experience, the fact of their pain carries real weight in my mind.
I notice that I can attend to multiple tasks even when something emotional is unresolved.
I tend to miss the social implications of who gets credit for an idea in a group.
After receiving bad news, I can feel the shock reverberating through my body for hours.
A friend's ongoing struggle rarely weighs on me.
I would trade personal recognition for the satisfaction of knowing my efforts lifted the team.
When resources are scarce, I instinctively direct them toward other people first.
I do not automatically read into people's tone or body language.
I enjoy being part of a group that evaluates ideas together without veto power.
I am the type who builds the team around my vision rather than the other way around.
I can tell when a meeting is happening for show rather than for any real decision-making.
I am somewhat more moved by other people's hardships than most people I know.
I tend to process grief in a measured, gradual way rather than in sudden, overwhelming waves.
Other people's suffering is mostly their concern, not mine.
When someone tells me about something painful that happened to them, I rarely feel any pull to comfort them.
I feel most productive when I have the freedom to shift direction at any moment.
I systematically review and update my plans as new information becomes available.
I commonly find myself the one editing and finalizing group deliverables.
I rarely register when someone raises their eyebrows briefly to acknowledge a shared understanding.
I can tell when two people have had a private conversation before a group meeting based on how they interact.
I routinely stockpile resources—savings, knowledge, connections—for my own future use.
I prefer to resolve disagreements through dialogue rather than any form of rank.
I would trade a comfortable retirement for the chance to fund someone else's education.
I routinely invest in education and training that advances my own skills.
I pre-read materials before classes, workshops, or events so I can engage more deeply.
I routinely track my personal progress and set benchmarks for my own improvement.
I enjoy the freedom that comes with not being the person in charge.
I trust that I can handle whatever comes up, so I don't waste time on contingency plans.
I am easily brought to goosebumps by music, words, or images that strike the right chord.
My emotional responses are proportional and consistent, which gives me a sense of reliability.
Thinking about suffering that future generations may face gives me a genuine wish to prevent it.
I shop and pack based on what occurs to me in the moment rather than from a list.
I find it rewarding to have the final word in a discussion.
